models_evaluated: AI dosing suggestion with simple feature-importance explanation (XAI)

links.outcome: Influence on clinician prescribing of AI with explanation versus AI alone
links.effect: Additional information (peer, AI, XAI) strongly influenced prescriptions, significantly for AI. Simple XAI did not have higher influence than AI alone; marginal impact of simple XAI was low.
links.quote: We found that additional information (peer, AI or XAI) had a strong influence on prescriptions (significantly for AI, not so for peers) but simple XAI did not have higher influence than AI alone.

links.outcome: Correlation between self-reported XAI usefulness and actual influence on prescriptions
links.effect: No correlation between clinicians' self-reported XAI usefulness and whether XAI influenced their prescriptions, casting doubt on self-reports as a valid metric for assessing XAI.
links.quote: There was no correlation between attitudes to AI or clinical experience on the AI-supported decisions and nor was there correlation between what doctors self-reported about how useful they found the XAI and whether the XAI actually influenced their prescriptions.

unlisted_practices: Comparing influence of peer-clinician information versus AI suggestions on prescribing decisions

models_evaluated: XAI suggestion using simple feature importance

links.effect: simple XAI did not have higher influence than AI alone; self-reported usefulness did not correlate with actual influence.
links.quote: Our findings suggest that the marginal impact of simple XAI was low in this setting and we also cast doubt on the utility of self-reports as a valid metric for assessing XAI in clinical experts.
